newsitem.title: USA: Texas girl has colon removed, ending legal dispute.
newsitem.headline: Texas girl has colon removed, ending legal dispute.

text.p: A bitter legal battle over parental rights in deciding medical treatment for sick children came to an end on Monday when a 10-year-old Texas girl finally received surgery to remove her diseased colon.

Rachel Stout, who suffers from potentially fatal ulcerative colitis, was operated on at Duke University Medical Centre in North Carolina, just one day after her parents relented to pressure and agreed to allow the surgery.

The operation ended a two-month battle for control of Rachel's treatment which saw her admitted to four hospitals amid a string of legal conflicts pitching the Stouts and parental rights groups against doctors and child welfare agencies.

The parents, Steve and Patricia Stout, repeatedly refused to give their permission for the surgical removal of Rachel's colon, saying they wanted to first try alternative methods such as drug therapy, laser treatment and dietary changes.
They finally gave in over the weekend after being told that Texas' Child Protection Services might be given custody of their daughter and itself order the surgery.

Larry Friedman, a lawyer representing the Stout family, told reporters in Dallas the operation went well and that Rachel was reported in good condition, although she will require two follow-up operations in coming months.
While the Stouts have come under intense criticism from authorities and even some family members, Friedman said on Monday they had only their daughter's best interests at heart.
"The Stouts have always wanted the highest and finest medical treatment for their daughter Rachel. They always knew that surgery was, for them, a last resort," he said.

Rachel's case drew widespread attention in early September when her father removed her from a children's hospital in Dallas with an intravenous tube still inserted in a major vein in her chest and flew her to Toronto for alternative laser treatment and aloe vera tonics.

Days later, Rachel contracted a fever and other Toronto doctors also urged surgery. She was sent back to Dallas and a state district judge granted joint custody to the Stouts and Child Protective Services, ruling that both sides be forced to accept the final opinion of independent medical experts.
Specialists at Duke University Medical Centre in Durham, North Carolina, last week recommended surgery, effectively forcing the Stouts to give up their fight or risk losing custody of Rachel.
The young girl is expected to be released from hospital in 10 to 14 days and allowed to return to her family's home near Fort Worth.
Parental rights groups have charged that state authorities were overzealous and had tried to take over the Stouts' role as parents.
